faq.q: What does an Instagram sale post template give my shop?
faq.a: A square that keeps the suitcase recognizable while the promotion is easy to read. The case can fill the frame, with the weekend price large enough to read on a phone.

faq.q: How do I make a sale post from one product photo?
faq.a: Upload a product photo, choose a sale scene, leave room for the offer you approved, and download the square. Check it on a phone, then post.

faq.q: Can the post show my discount and the event date large enough to read?
faq.a: Yes. The layout is there so the promotion leads. You type the offer, the code, and the dates that match the sale you approved, then read them back before the post goes up.

faq.q: What size is the sale image so it fits an Instagram feed?
faq.a: Square, which fits an Instagram or Facebook feed post. For a wide site header, place that square on a wider background in your design tool.

faq.q: Can I reuse one scene for a later promotion without a new photo?
faq.a: Yes. Keep the product scene and change the headline. One week can be a price cut, and the next can be a different approved line.

faq.q: Can I turn the sale square into a tall Story I can post?
faq.a: The template gives you a square. For a tall Story or Reel, set that square on a 9:16 background after download.

faq.q: Where should the discount code go so shoppers can read it?
faq.a: In the open part of the layout, as text you can still edit. Read the full offer on a phone-sized preview before the ad runs.

faq.q: How many credits does a sale photo use before I download it?
faq.a: Each photo costs 24 credits. The cost is shown before you start, and a failed job returns those credits. The download has no watermark. You can use it in your ads, pages, and posts.

faq.q: What should I do with the square when the sale ends?
faq.a: Pause or replace the post so an old date or code is not still up. The product scene can stay for a later promotion or as a plain listing image.

faq.q: Can I start from a holiday scene and swap the offer later?
faq.a: Yes. Keep the suitcase scene and swap the headline when the holiday passes. The product photo underneath can be used again.

faq.q: Do I need a paid plan before I can post a sale square?
faq.a: Yes. Starter is $24.50 a month for 200 credits, Pro is $35 for 300, and Premium is $63 for 600. Photos, batches, and API jobs all draw from that balance.

reviews.h2: Sale Scenes Sellers Build from One Photo
reviews.lead: A few ways sellers use one product photo as the scene behind an offer.

items.d: The shop generates a seasonal scene and types the percent, code and end date in its editor. When the number changes, the text you added changes and the product scene can stay.

items.t: End date kept out of the file
items.d: The end date is not generated into the image, so an expired promotion is removed by deleting the text you added. The product photo underneath can be reused.
The same scene carries a percent-off line in one ad and a different approved line in another. Both lines are added after download.
An empty area is left for the code, then checked on a phone-sized preview before the ad is published. The code is typed later, not asked for in the picture.
The square image goes in a Facebook or Instagram feed, or on the product page, after the final offer is added. A wide site header means placing it on a wider background in the editor.

items.t: No new shoot for the event
items.d: They start from a product photo they already have instead of booking a banner shoot. Claims and offer terms stay their responsibility.

definition.title: What a Sale Post Does in the Feed
paras: It is the square you post when the suitcase price changes for a long weekend. The case stays fully visible, and the end date sits in the empty area beside the case.
You are filling a feed square, not drawing one from scratch. Next month the same suitcase can carry a new headline for a different event.

reasons.h2: A Sale Square Shoppers Can Read
reasons.lead: The square should make the promotion obvious to someone scrolling past the shop.

items.d: Someone scrolling should see the suitcase offer before they study the handle. The case stays in the frame so the shopper still knows what is on sale.
The feed frame is already composed. You set the suitcase in it, and the open area is already where the offer should sit.
Use the suitcase square on the feed and again on the product page. When the next event starts, only the headline changes, so the shop still looks like the same shop.
